fields.Front: How are composite and multi-valued attributes handled when mapping an entity to a table?
fields.Back:
COMPOSITE: include only its SIMPLE COMPONENT attributes - 'we don't turn Name into a column; we turn FirstName and LastName into columns'.
MULTI-VALUED: do NOT put it in the entity's table at all - it gets its own table (rule 6).

fields.Front: Map PROFESSOR with attributes EmpID (key), Office, Ext and composite Name(FirstName, LastName), and say what the rows and columns mean.
fields.Back: PROFESSOR(EmpID, FirstName, LastName, Office, Ext), primary key EmpID. With data: six professors give six rows, five attributes give five columns, and 'each row is a tuple that represents an actual thing in our world'. Sample row: Laura Reid, 11, ST238, 86905. Column order does not matter.

fields.Front: Library example: write the three tables, and what counting habit does the instructor use first?
fields.Back:
Count first: 'I've got three entities, so I'm going to need three tables. Book has five attributes, Publisher three, Member six.'
Book (Book_ID, Title, Price, Author, Available)
Publisher (Pub_ID, Name, Address)
Member (Member_ID, Member_date, Member_price, Address, Name, Expiry_date)
Underline the key 'to indicate that it's the thing that's going to force each row to be unique'.

fields.Text: Design goes from the real world (mini-world) to a {{c1::model (the ER diagram)}} to a {{c1::relational database}}, which may use only four data structures: {{c1::tables}}, rows, columns and cells.

'The first rule I want you to get from this': each {{c1::entity}} becomes a {{c1::table}}, its {{c1::attributes}} become the columns, each entity instance becomes a row, and the entity's key becomes the primary key.

When mapping an entity, a {{c1::composite}} attribute contributes only its {{c1::simple components}} (FirstName and LastName, not Name), and a {{c1::multi-valued}} attribute is not put in the entity's table at all.
